In every federal bureaucracy, there is bloat; managers who do nothing outnumber those actually working. This is true across all federal organizations in America. The ratio of managers and supervisors to other employees illustrates this well.

Evaluation in such bureaucracies is subjective: managers evaluate themselves and their friends, often giving outstanding reviews. In government jobs, 62-64% received outstanding evaluations, while only 47% of non-managerial staff did. This suggests a rigged system where managers' self-evaluations overshadow those of the actual workers.

Similarly, in hospitals, the number of administrators is skyrocketing compared to doctors. The growth in administrators drives up healthcare costs, making healthcare unaffordable in the United States due to the sheer number of non-contributing staff.

Managers are always devising new ways to exploit their positions. For instance, health insurance companies deny a third (32%) of claims, often doing so as a tactic to force patients into negotiation, where they might agree to pay back disputed amounts.

In France, Kafka wrote "The Trial," published before World War I. The book's protagonist, Joseph K., works at a bank and is arrested without cause. He faces a trial with no explanation of his wrongdoing. The purpose, as Kafka suggests, is to prosecute innocent people in meaningless trials. This bureaucracy leads to corruption because it provides busywork for officials who would rather target the compliant than deal with potentially combative criminals.

In Toronto, I allowed my four-year-old son to run around the park after two months of trust-building.
